newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela satisified with progress in Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Mandela satisified with progress in Zaire talks.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela believes South Africa's efforts to broker an end to Zaire's civil war made a solid start in his talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, his spokesman said on Thursday.
"The president was satisfied with the discussion," Joel Netshitenzhe told Reuters of the hour-long meeting Mandela had with Kabila in Cape Town on Wednesday night.
Netshitenzhe said the talks had explored possible new initiatives to end the fighting between Kabila's rebel force and troops of President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Officials did not expect Mandela to take part in any further talks, which might go ahead on Thursday. U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun is also in the city.
Kabila could soon meet the man he is trying to topple, sources close to the talks said. Representatives of Mobutu were in Cape Town but it was not clear if they would meet Kabila, the sources said.
In Kinshasa, Zairean Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba told a news conference Mobutu and Kabila could meet directly once their envoys had consulted.
"Things are getting clearer. Plans are afoot for a meeting between the head of state and the rebel leader. This meeting is imminent," Kin-Kiey said.
Such a meeting would bring a sigh of relief in the Zaire capital of Kinshasa.
A senior South African source said Mandela wanted to bring Mobutu and Kabila together in South Africa as part of his efforts to make peace in Zaire.

Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Aziz Pahad was instrumental in arranging earlier talks in South Africa between representatives of the Zairean rivals and was expected to be involved in any new arrangements.

Kabila arrived in Cape Town from Lubumbashi, Zaire's second city which rebels seized last week after only token resistance from Mobutu's troops. The rebels now hold more than half of the mineral-rich country.
Speaking to reporters before leaving Lubumbashi, Kabila appeared to dampen hopes for averting war in teeming Kinshasa, home to five million people.
"There will be no ceasefire until Mobutu relinquishes power," he said.
Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, had earlier told Reuters by telephone the "people are against a ceasefire".
"The people do not want a ceasefire, they want an end to this corrupt regime," said Kabila. That heightened fear of a tragedy in Kinshasa should rebel forces reach the capital.
After crippling Kinshasa with an anti-Mobutu protest action on Monday and Tuesday, Zaire's main opposition called a meeting of its leadership on Wednesday to plan further measures.
"We will launch new measures for the coming week. The action will continue," declared Mukendi wa Kamanda, chief political aide to opposition stalwart Etienne Tshisekedi.

Shops and businesses reopened on Wednesday and the city regained its normal pace after a well-observed stay-at-home protest on Monday. Police thwarted a student protest march on Tuesday but Kinshasa residents stayed at home.

Kabila's rebels say they are 300 km (180 miles) from Kinshasa, a claim ridiculed by the government. But given the inability of Zaire's undisciplined army to offer resistance, many Zaireans doubt government forces can hold Kinshasa.
